Few ethical questions in modern science are as hard as whether animals should be used in research. Advocates note that animal studies have played a part in almost every major medical breakthrough, vaccines and cancer therapies among them, and that cell cultures and computer models still can't answer many questions about whole living organisms. Human suffering would probably grow without this work.

Opponents counter that animals feel pain and fear, and that their suffering isn't justified merely because another species gains from it. They add that findings in animals don't always carry over to people.

The sensible view sits somewhere between the two poles. Animal research can be defended when it is genuinely needed, when nothing else can substitute, and when suffering is kept as low as possible. The broadly accepted "Three Rs" principles, Replacement, Reduction and Refinement, express this idea. Society should keep funding alternatives so that, gradually, fewer animals are required at all.

The cleric is the textbook support character in tabletop role-playing games such as Dungeons & Dragons and in many MMOs. Parties recruit one because clerics handle tasks that few other classes can.

**Why parties want a cleric**

- **Healing.** During and after fights, clerics bring hit points back, so fighters and other front-line characters can last through longer battles.
- **Recovery from disaster.** They cure poison, disease and curses, and at high levels they can even raise fallen characters from the dead.
- **Buffs and protection.** Spells such as Bless or Shield of Faith help the whole team hit more often and get hit less.
- **Handling undead.** A cleric can turn or destroy undead monsters, which takes much of the danger out of some dungeons.
- **Flexibility.** Plenty of clerics wear sturdy armor and can fight in melee, so they don't have to stay hidden in the back row.

**What happens without one**

A party can certainly get by with no cleric, but it must adjust:

- Healing potions become the group's crutch, and they cost gold and eventually run out.
- Characters have to rest more frequently, which may let enemies regroup or cause a time-limited quest to expire.
- Other classes, like druids, bards or paladins, might take on healing duty part of the time.
- Characters die more often, and the death can be permanent when no one can cast revival magic.
- Players grow more careful, avoid risky encounters, and lean harder on stealth or diplomacy.

In most current games, a cleric isn't strictly necessary, but it acts as a safety net. Remove it and each mistake costs more, which some groups welcome as an extra challenge.

**DEEPLY SORRY**

*Genre:* Comedy
*Starring:* Jim Carrey
*Tone:* *Liar Liar* crossed with *The Mask*, with the warmth of *The Truman Show*

---

**Logline**

The most successful professional apologizer in the world, a man hired to take the fall for the rich and famous, learns that he has never genuinely said sorry for anything. He has seven days to figure out how, before he loses the one person who ever believed in him.

---

**Synopsis**

**Walt Fennimore** (Jim Carrey) is gifted: no one says "I'm sorry" the way Walt does. He can cry on command, drop to his knees in a heartbreaking show of remorse, and give a tearful public statement so affecting that audiences forget what the scandal was.

A decade ago, Walt was an unsuccessful regional theater actor. He took a temp job reading a politician's apology aloud at a press conference, and the footage went viral. These days he runs **Mea Culpa Inc.**, a boutique agency that hires him out to celebrities, CEOs and influencers. If a pop star insults an entire country, Walt arrives as her "personal spiritual advisor" and claims responsibility for "writing the tweet." If a tech billionaire's self-driving lawnmower terrorizes a retirement community, Walt plays the "rogue engineer" who reprogrammed it. He has been fired, publicly humiliated, and theatrically walked out of buildings more than four hundred times. He holds a loyalty card at the paparazzi's favorite coffee shop.

Walt is wealthy, loud and utterly shameless. He is also lonely, though he'd never say so.

The one person who can see through him is his ex-wife, **Nora** (a warm, grounded part that would suit an actress like Rachel McAdams). She teaches music at a public school, and their 12-year-old daughter, **Pip**, has picked up Walt's taste for drama. Walt skips Pip's recitals, forgets birthdays, and papers over each failure with a dazzling, theatrical apology that means nothing. Nora has run out of patience. By the end of the week she is moving to Toronto with Pip.

---

**The Hook**

Walt lands the biggest client of his career. **Chase Dunmore** (a smug, scene-stealing villain part) is a tech mogul whose company caused a blackout across an entire city. Chase pays Walt seven figures to pose as the employee at fault. There's a complication: Pip's school orchestra was playing at the concert hall that lost power, and Pip spent three hours stuck in an elevator. Walt can't accept blame for harming his own daughter.

Then something odd occurs. After a run-in with a mysterious elderly janitor at the concert hall (a small, magical cameo), Walt discovers he **physically can't apologize** for anything he didn't do. Whenever he tries to fake one, his body rebels. His face twists into grotesque grimaces, his limbs lock into contortions, and his voice breaks into gibberish. On live television he attempts Chase's apology and ends up performing an involuntary interpretive dance across the press-room table.

This is the central comic engine. It gives Carrey a reason for the elastic, all-out physical comedy that made *Ace Ventura* and *Liar Liar* iconic, while the emotional stakes keep the story grounded.

---

**Act Two**

His business falls apart. Every celebrity he has ever covered for crawls out of the woodwork and demands that he "fix" their latest scandals. Chase hires a ruthless replacement apologizer and launches a smear campaign to turn Walt into the scapegoat for the blackout regardless.

In desperation, Walt works out that the curse lets him apologize only for things he really did. He sets out to deliver **real** apologies to the people he has wronged: Nora, Pip, his estranged brother, a former theater castmate whose big break he stole, and a coffee shop barista he has tipped exactly one cent since 2014. Every apology is harder and funnier than the one before, since Walt has no clue how to be sincere without performing. In one standout sequence, he must apologize to a children's birthday party he once ruined while dressed as a hot dog, and he does so while dressed as a hot dog.

Gradually, the man who could fake any emotion begins to feel real ones.

---

**Act Three**

Nora's departure is a day away and Chase is about to escape justice, so Walt uses his talents one last time, now in service of the truth. He crashes Chase's televised "Corporate Responsibility Summit" and stages an elaborate, chaotic performance. It tricks Chase into confessing in public, and then leaves the billionaire twitching uncontrollably as he tries to fake his own apology. The curse, it turns out, is contagious.

Walt dashes to Pip's rescheduled recital, misses the opening, and slips in quietly at the back. Then he does the most radical thing he has ever done. He makes no scene. He simply watches and listens.

Afterward, he offers Nora and Pip a brief, plain, unrehearsed apology. Nora doesn't take him back right away, but she delays the move. In the final scene, Walt launches a new business called **Sorry School**, where he teaches people to apologize sincerely. On day one, his sole student is Chase Dunmore.

---

**Why It Works for Carrey**

*Deeply Sorry* hands Carrey a hero who is a nonstop human cartoon on the surface and a broken man underneath, which is precisely the blend behind his biggest hits. The concept is high, the lines are endlessly quotable, and the physical set pieces are made for trailers. It is also a comedy about public shame and accountability in the internet age. That timeliness would make it feel fresh instead of nostalgic, and it could return Carrey to where he belongs: the center of a crowd-pleasing summer comedy.

When test utterances are short, speaker verification suffers considerably, because i-vectors taken from limited speech vary widely and are less reliable. In this paper we present a way to convert short-utterance i-vectors into representations that look more like those from long utterances, using a conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN). The generator takes the short-utterance i-vector as its condition and is trained to output the matching long-utterance i-vector, and the discriminator learns to tell generated vectors apart from real ones. To keep speaker identity intact, we pair the adversarial objective with a reconstruction loss and a speaker-discriminative constraint. We run experiments on the NIST Speaker Recognition Evaluation corpus using test segments of different lengths. The transformed i-vectors lower equal error rates consistently compared with conventional PLDA baselines, and the biggest improvements appear for the shortest utterances.

Our subject is a family of semi-linear elliptic boundary value problems whose nonlinear production term carries a spatially varying scaling coefficient. Such a structure shows up in models of reaction–diffusion, population dynamics and heat generation. These problems typically have no closed-form solution, and standard Newton-type methods need expensive Jacobian evaluations, so we put forward a linearization approach that swaps the nonlinear problem for a series of linear elliptic ones. At each step, the iterate comes from solving a linear equation whose coefficients depend only on the preceding approximation, and a stabilization parameter is selected based on the Lipschitz constant of the nonlinearity. Given appropriate assumptions on the scaling function and the source, we prove that the iteration is well defined and converges strongly in H¹ to the unique weak solution, and we obtain an a priori error estimate that shows geometric convergence. Numerical experiments using a finite element discretization back up the theory and demonstrate how efficient the method is.

This is extremely common, and it says less about whether you understand sleep than about how your brain trades off the present against the future.

**1. "Revenge bedtime procrastination"**
When your days are crammed with obligations (work, school, family, what everyone else needs), late at night may be the only time that feels like yours. Staying awake turns into a way to take back some freedom, even if what you're doing isn't especially enjoyable. Going to bed feels like surrendering the day to your responsibilities again.

**2. Costs come later, rewards come now**
One more episode or a little more scrolling pays off immediately. Tiredness is a problem for "tomorrow you," who seems like a slightly different and more abstract person. Simply knowing something is bad for you rarely outweighs a reward you're holding right now.

**3. Tiredness erodes self-control**
As the night goes on you get more worn out, and disciplined choices get harder. Ironically, the moment when you most need willpower to set the phone down is the moment you have the least.

**4. Screens are built to hold you**
Autoplay, endless feeds and notifications take away the natural places to stop. At no point does the content tell you "that's enough."

**5. Your body clock may run late**
Some people truly have a later chronotype, so they don't get sleepy until late. Bright screens in the evening can push that clock later still.

**6. Avoidance**
At times, bedtime is when worries surface. Keeping busy holds anxious thoughts off.

**What tends to help**
- Give yourself genuine free time earlier in the evening, so the night doesn't have to make up for it.
- Set a "wind-down" alarm 30–60 minutes before bed, in addition to your wake-up alarm.
- Charge your phone outside the bedroom, or at the very least on the far side of the room.
- Make your bedtime routine enjoyable (a book, a shower, music) so you're heading toward it instead of giving something up for it.
- Wake at a consistent time, weekends included; over time that drags your bedtime earlier.

If the pattern continues despite these changes, or you lie awake and can't fall asleep, consider speaking with a doctor about insomnia or a circadian rhythm problem.

The first thing I did as president was sign an executive order that made every federal employee take a forty-minute nap at 2 p.m.

Let me explain. I became president by accident. It began as a joke on a bass-fishing forum, a write-in campaign, and by the time people took it seriously I had won thirty-one states. Four days into office I found out that the president is briefed at 6:30 every morning and that no one would let me skip it. I wanted out, and impeachment looked like the quickest way.

Nap Time was in place for two weeks when the Department of Labor announced that federal productivity had climbed eighteen percent. Workplace accidents fell. Half of the Fortune 500 took up the policy on their own. My approval rating went up nine points.

Fine. I raised the stakes.

I posted Air Force One on an online auction site, described as "big plane, runs great, some missiles removed." A tech billionaire bought it for 1.3 billion dollars and also agreed to pay for its maintenance. Economists called it the most efficient asset sale in American history. A cable news segment asked, "Is He a Genius?"

By now I was desperate. I skipped the State of the Union and livestreamed myself reading every bill Congress had sent me, word for word, in a monotone, stopping each time I reached something I didn't understand. It ran eleven hours. Sixty million people tuned in. Three senators resigned after I got to page 840 of the farm bill and asked out loud why a golf course was getting a subsidy.

For my last try, I sent my mother to negotiate a trade deal with China. She had no diplomatic background, but she had spent forty years running the church bake sale. She returned with tariff cuts, a panda loan, and the premier's scallion pancake recipe, which she has since improved.

Last week the House Judiciary Committee finally met to discuss me. I watched from the couch in the Oval Office, full of hope.

They voted unanimously to propose a constitutional amendment that would give me a third term.

I'm going to take a nap.

**Nigerians Vote in Tight Presidential Race Amid Fears Over Disputed Result**

LAGOS, Nigeria — On Saturday, millions of Nigerians queued at polling stations to pick between President Goodluck Jonathan, the incumbent, and Muhammadu Buhari, a former military ruler. Analysts say it may be the most tightly contested election since the return to civilian rule in 1999.

The contest sets Jonathan, of the People's Democratic Party (PDP), which has dominated for a long time, against Buhari, a retired major general who heads the All Progressives Congress (APC), an alliance of opposition parties founded in 2013. For the first time since military rule ended, an opposition candidate is widely viewed as having a real chance of ousting a sitting president.

In many places voting began slowly, as election officials wrestled with new biometric card readers meant to reduce fraud. At his own polling unit in his home state of Bayelsa, Jonathan could not be verified by a card reader and had to be accredited by hand. The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) let voting continue into Sunday in some places affected by technical glitches.

The election was first set for Feb. 14 but was delayed six weeks after security chiefs said they couldn't guarantee safety in the northeast, where the Islamist militant group Boko Haram has fought a six-year insurgency that has killed thousands and uprooted more than a million people.

Security has been the dominant campaign theme. Buhari, who ruled Nigeria briefly in the 1980s after a coup, has cast himself as a disciplined leader able to defeat the insurgents and root out corruption. Jonathan's backers cite recent military gains against Boko Haram and economic growth during his time in office, although falling oil prices have squeezed government revenue and weakened the naira.

The race also mirrors Nigeria's long-running regional and religious divisions. Buhari is a Muslim and draws much of his support from the mostly Muslim north, whereas Jonathan, a Christian, is strongest in the south, including the oil-producing Niger Delta.

Those divisions have raised fears that the losing side might refuse to accept the outcome. After the 2011 election, which Jonathan won against Buhari, rioting in parts of the north left about 800 people dead, according to Human Rights Watch.

In January, the two candidates signed an accord in Abuja promising to campaign peacefully and honor the result, yet tensions remain high. Some militants in the Niger Delta have cautioned that there will be unrest if Jonathan loses, and some Buhari supporters have sworn to resist any result they regard as rigged.

International observers, among them teams from the African Union and the European Union, are watching the vote, and world leaders have called on Nigerians to keep the process peaceful.

INEC chairman Attahiru Jega has said that results will be collated at state level and then announced in Abuja, with official figures due in the next few days.

An outright win requires a simple majority of votes nationwide plus at least 25 percent of the vote in two-thirds of Nigeria's 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory.

Subject: Concern about EBS

Hi [Name],

Last week, while going through our AWS account, I noticed a handful of problems in the way we use EBS (Elastic Block Store). Taken one by one, none is an emergency, but together they mean wasted spend and a genuine security risk, so I'd like to bring them up ahead of our next infrastructure review.

**Unattached volumes.** [number] volumes are sitting in the "available" state, which means no instance is using them. Most seem to be remnants of instances shut down during last quarter's migration. We continue to pay for all that storage, around [$X] a month.

**Unencrypted volumes.** Encryption at rest is turned off on several production volumes, some of them attached to our database servers. That goes against our data-handling policy and an audit would almost surely flag it.

**Snapshot sprawl.** Our snapshots have no lifecycle policy, and some are more than two years old. Quite a few were taken from volumes that no longer exist.

**Outdated volume types.** Most of our volumes still use gp2. Switching to gp3 would reduce storage cost by roughly 20% per GB and allow performance to be provisioned separately from volume size. The change can be done in place with no downtime.

Suggested next steps:

- Confirm who owns the unattached volumes, snapshot each one a last time, and delete whatever isn't needed
- Turn on EBS encryption by default for new volumes and plan a migration for the unencrypted ones that exist
- Configure Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager policies so snapshot retention is handled automatically
- Roll out the gp2-to-gp3 change in stages, beginning with non-production environments

Before Thursday's meeting, I can put together a complete inventory and cost estimate. If any of these volumes are set up this way deliberately, for reasons I don't know about, let me know so I can factor them in.

Thanks,
[Your Name]

**The Wall at Okafor's**

Each Sunday morning, stories filled the brick wall next to Okafor's Laundromat.

No one could say precisely how it began. One week a lone index card was thumbtacked to the corkboard by the door, six lines about a cat who thought she was a lighthouse. By the next Sunday there were eleven. By the close of that summer the board had stretched along the entire side of the building, and people came from three neighborhoods just to read it.

A strip of plywood at the top carried the one rule, painted on: LEAVE A STORY, LEAVE A COMMENT.

Comments went on sticky notes under each card. Most were kind. *Loved the ending. Who is the woman in the blue coat? Please write more about the cat.*

Some were unkind, and that was where Mrs. Okafor came in.

She had owned the laundromat for thirty-one years. Each Sunday evening she went down the length of the wall carrying a coffee can, taking off the cruel notes, the ads, and the cards that were really just phone numbers. She pinned back anything the wind had shaken loose. When rain was in the forecast, she draped a plastic tarp over the board. She never wrote a word herself.

Theo had been leaving stories since April, always unsigned, always on green cards so he could spot them again. He was fifteen and had never told a soul that he wrote. He read every comment on his cards twice, first fast and then slowly.

In October, a new card showed up at the top of the wall, in Mrs. Okafor's careful block capitals.

MY KNEES ARE GETTING OLD AND THE WALL IS GETTING BIG. I NEED HELP KEEPING IT. IF YOU LOVE THIS PLACE, COME INSIDE AND ASK.

Within a day, sticky notes crowded beneath it. *We love you, Mrs. O! Thank you for everything. Someone should totally do this.*

No one came inside.

That Sunday, Theo stood in front of the card for a long while. Then he pulled a green index card from his pocket, wrote three words, and pinned it under hers.

*I'll do it.*

As he pushed the door open, the dryers were humming, and Mrs. Okafor was already holding out a second coffee can.

"How did you know it was me?" he asked.

"Who do you think," she said, "has been keeping the rain off your stories since April?"

**Form 22-B**

Good morning, Madam Chair and members of the Committee. I am Eleanor Whitcombe, and I have come to present Form 22-B, Request for Exercise of Lifetime Termination Allowance. The three required copies are with me, each one signed and witnessed.

I have studied the guidance with care. Section 4 obliges me to show grave and lasting harm, the lack of any adequate legal remedy, and a reasonable expectation that the individual I name will do further harm. I shall take each criterion in order.

Regarding harm: fourteen months ago my son, Thomas, was terminated under an approved allowance. The petitioner had worked beside him for six weeks. She stated her grounds as follows: Thomas had "ruined her prospects" by reporting her to their employer for falsifying safety inspections.

Regarding remedy: I have lodged three appeals. All were dismissed because approved terminations are final and cannot be reviewed.

Regarding future harm: since then, the individual I am naming has voted to approve forty-one more requests, nine of them involving employees who had reported misconduct.

That individual is Councillor Martin Hale, who is seated second from your left.

I observe that the Councillor has turned rather pale.

I direct the Committee's attention to Rule 9, under which any member named in a petition must recuse himself at once. I would also note that Councillor Brand is absent today because of illness. Once Councillor Hale recuses himself, four members are left. Under Rule 12, if a quorum of five cannot be kept, any pending petition is considered approved when the session ends.

I have taken the liberty of checking the clock. The session ends in six minutes.

I have nothing further to say, Madam Chair. I am content to wait.

Because color screening above the deconfinement transition is expected to weaken or break up bound charm-anticharm pairs, charmonium is a sensitive probe of the quark-gluon plasma created in relativistic heavy-ion collisions. This study examines how the J/ψ, χc and ψ′ behave inside the medium at temperatures higher than the critical temperature Tc. We use a nonrelativistic potential model whose temperature-dependent heavy-quark potential is fixed by lattice QCD free-energy data, and from it we calculate the binding energy, radius and dissociation temperature of every state. The spectral functions that result are then set against lattice correlator calculations. Our results show that the excited states dissolve near the transition, while the J/ψ can remain bound up to about 1.5–2 Tc, a range that hinges on which potential is adopted. We also discuss what this means for sequential suppression and for charmonium regeneration in heavy-ion experiments.

This paper explores tunneling in a bosonic Josephson junction, built from a Bose–Einstein condensate held in a double-well potential, where a single-mode optical cavity field assists the tunneling between the wells. Working in a two-mode approximation, we obtain an effective Hamiltonian in which the tunneling amplitude is set by the number of photons inside the cavity, which gives a nonlinear system of coupled atoms and light. We follow how the population imbalance and the relative phase between the wells evolve, using both a mean-field description and a fully quantum one. The cavity field turns out to act as a tunable control parameter able to switch the system between Josephson oscillations and macroscopic quantum self-trapping. The nonlinearity that the cavity introduces also produces bistability and alters the collapse-and-revival dynamics. In addition, the light transmitted through the cavity serves as a nondestructive probe of how the atoms tunnel.

Our subject is the capacity of the q-ary deletion channel. Here every symbol from an alphabet of size q is removed independently with probability d, and the receiver sees the symbols that remain, in order, with no information about where they originally sat. The binary version of this channel has received a great deal of attention, but far less is understood about the non-binary case, and for no nontrivial deletion probability is there a closed-form capacity expression. We present a new upper bound on the capacity of the q-ary deletion channel that holds for any q ≥ 2. The method relies on giving the receiver genie-aided side information about the deletion process, so that the original channel becomes a memoryless one whose capacity can be evaluated numerically with the Blahut–Arimoto algorithm. We demonstrate that exploiting the run structure of non-binary input sequences yields a tighter reduction than simply extending the existing binary arguments. For every deletion probability, the resulting bound is strictly better than the trivial erasure-channel bound of (1 − d) log q, and the improvement is greatest for small alphabets and high deletion rates. The difference between our bound and the erasure bound also shrinks to zero as q increases, which matches known asymptotic results. Numerical results for a number of alphabet sizes show how much we improve on previously published bounds.

**The Wrong Century**

Mara Okafor's last memory was of the lab countdown hitting zero and somebody shouting about a voltage spike. What she became aware of next was the smell of damp straw, woodsmoke and something far worse, which she would later find out was a pigsty.

She pushed herself upright in a muddy field. Somewhere a church bell rang. Behind a stone wall, two boys in coarse wool tunics gaped at her, and one of them made the sign of the cross.

Her wrist display had gone dark. Her phone showed no signal. She looked again, which accomplished nothing, and then she burst out laughing, since the only other option was to scream.

The shape of the church tower and the words the boys yelled as they fled suggested England to her, sometime in the 1300s. She had taken exactly one semester on the period in college, and what she mostly recalled was that people died of ailments that were simple to treat in her own day.

Her first lesson came within a week: knowledge does no good if you cannot account for where it came from. She told the village reeve to boil the drinking water, and he stared as though she had proposed baptizing the well. So she quit explaining and just did it where everyone could see. She brewed thin ale the way the villagers did, because brewing meant boiling too. She scrubbed her hands so often that the baker's wife began calling her "the clean woman," and not kindly.

The second lesson was slower to arrive: everything takes time. A letter meant hunting down someone who could read. Starting a fire cost her twenty minutes and three burned fingers, until old Agnes, the widow who had reluctantly given her a roof, showed her how to use flint and dry fungus. Mara had once helped design parts of a quantum relay. Now a woman who could not write her own name was teaching her, and Agnes was the better teacher.

Nothing streamed, nothing scrolled, and there was nothing to fill the quiet. Evenings were long and dark, so people talked. They swapped stories, sang, and quarreled over the weather and the lord's new taxes. Mara realized she could recall more of her grandmother's old songs than she ever had back in her own century, and she started singing them by the fire. The children adored them.

She got things wrong. Once she set a broken arm with too much confidence and nearly got herself accused of witchcraft. The miller saved her by testifying that he had watched her pray at Mass. After that she presented every useful idea as something "my mother's people did," and let others claim the credit if they wished.

By midsummer her palms were callused. She could sense coming rain from the ache in the air and the flight of the swallows. She knew which herbs Agnes used against fever and which were only for show.

One autumn evening a strange shimmer opened at the edge of the field where she had first woken, and her dead wrist display blinked back to life. *Retrieval window: 90 seconds.*

Mara stood in the doorway of Agnes's cottage for a long while. Then she stepped inside, kissed the old woman on the forehead, and walked toward the light, holding a pouch of dried yarrow that she had no plan to explain to anyone back home.

The interviews were not going well.

Candidate one, a hedge fund manager called Bradley, took twenty minutes to describe how he would "scale suffering" and "disrupt the afterlife vertical." The Devil scribbled *no* on his legal pad and underlined it twice.

Candidate two, a former dictator, mostly wanted to ask about the dental plan. Candidate three had once replied-all to a company email sent to forty thousand people. The Devil admired the impulse but felt he lacked follow-through.

"They all want the fire," he said to Asmodeus, his assistant of nine thousand years, once the dictator had left. "The pitchforks. The screaming. Not one of them understands that the fire was never the point."

"Then what was, sir?"

The Devil rubbed his horns. He was weary, and had been since about the Renaissance. "Patience. True torment is patient. It is quiet. It grinds you down with one small, reasonable-sounding obstacle after another, until you forget you ever wanted anything."

Asmodeus consulted the clipboard. "There's one more applicant. She wasn't on the list. She, er, let herself in."

"She?"

"The posting did say 'man,' sir. She has submitted a written objection."

The woman who walked in had on a beige cardigan and a lanyard. Nobody invited her to sit, and she sat anyway, opened a manila folder, and pushed a form across the desk.

"You'll need to fill this out before we start," she said. "Black ink. Not blue. Blue gets rejected."

The Devil studied the form. It ran eleven pages. Section 4 wanted every prior address, including any from before the universe was created. Section 7 sent him to Section 9, and Section 9 sent him back to Section 7.

"And your present occupation," he said slowly, "is what?"

"Department of Motor Vehicles. Window six. Twenty-two years." She checked her watch. "You should take a number."

He took one. It was 847. On the wall, a small screen that had not been there a moment earlier flickered on: NOW SERVING 12.

For the first time in four thousand years, the Devil felt a chill run down his spine. He glanced at Asmodeus, who nodded with wide eyes.

"When could you start?" the Devil asked.

She kept her eyes on the folder. "Your application is incomplete," she said. "Come back Tuesday."

Underwater archaeology, sometimes called maritime or nautical archaeology when it concentrates on ships and seafaring, takes the methods of land-based fieldwork into a setting that is punishing for both people and equipment. Poor visibility, powerful currents, cold, pressure and very limited time on the bottom all restrict what researchers can achieve. At the same time, these conditions can preserve organic materials, including hull timbers, rope, textiles and food remains, that rarely last on land. Since becoming a scientific discipline in the 1960s, the field has built up a refined toolkit for finding, recording, recovering and conserving submerged cultural heritage.

## Locating Sites

Research usually starts in the archives. Shipping records, insurance claims, old charts, and accounts from fishermen or sponge divers often shrink the search area; sponge divers were the first to find both the Antikythera wreck and the Late Bronze Age wreck at Uluburun, off the southern coast of Turkey. After that, systematic survey depends mainly on remote sensing:

- **Side-scan sonar** creates detailed acoustic images of the seafloor that show hull outlines, ballast mounds and scattered cargo.
- **Multibeam echosounders** collect high-resolution bathymetric data, from which three-dimensional terrain models can be built.
- **Sub-bottom profilers** send out lower-frequency acoustic pulses that pass through sediment and reveal structures buried under the seabed.
- **Marine magnetometers** pick up the magnetic anomalies caused by iron objects such as anchors, cannon and fastenings.
- **Airborne LiDAR bathymetry and satellite imagery** can chart shallow, clear coastal waters over very large areas.

Targets flagged by these surveys are then checked by eye, using either divers or remotely operated vehicles.

## Accessing the Site

In fairly shallow water, typically under about 50 meters, archaeologists can work on the seabed themselves with SCUBA or surface-supplied air. Mixed-gas diving and closed-circuit rebreathers allow greater depth and longer work periods, though they bring higher cost, more complexity and greater physiological risk. Below those limits, robotic systems become essential. Remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) are connected by a tether to a surface ship and carry high-definition cameras, lights and manipulator arms able to recover objects delicately. Autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) follow pre-programmed survey patterns and gather sonar and photographic data over wide areas without constant human control. The Black Sea Maritime Archaeology Project, for instance, used this technology to document dozens of wrecks lying in deep, oxygen-poor water, including a roughly 2,400-year-old Greek merchant ship that is almost perfectly preserved.

## Recording and Documentation

Since excavation inevitably destroys context, careful recording is the foundation of all scientific work underwater. Conventional methods include baseline-offset measurement, trilateration from fixed control points, and rigid grid frames, with divers sketching on waterproof drafting film. Digital methods have increasingly added to these techniques and often replaced them. Photogrammetry, also known as structure-from-motion, merges thousands of overlapping photographs into accurate 3D models that can be measured; acoustic positioning systems give individual finds geographic coordinates; and underwater laser scanners record fine surface detail. The data that result can be analyzed long after the fieldwork ends and let the public explore sites virtually.

## Excavation and Recovery

When excavation is justified, sediment is cleared with airlifts or water dredges, which work like underwater vacuum cleaners, and the removed material is run through sieves to catch small finds. Delicate deposits are exposed by fanning the water over them by hand. Lifting bags raise heavy objects, and in shallow water a cofferdam can be built around a site so it can be dug dry, which is what happened with La Salle's ship *La Belle* in Texas in the 1990s. Occasionally whole hulls have been lifted, most famously the Swedish warship *Vasa* in 1961 and Henry VIII's warship *Mary Rose* in 1982.

## Scientific Analysis

Laboratories apply many techniques to the recovered material. Dendrochronology can date ship timbers and show where the trees were cut, and radiocarbon dating is used on other organic remains. Lead-isotope and elemental analyses help identify where metals and ceramics came from, while analysis of organic residues and ancient DNA can reveal what amphorae once held. X-ray radiography and computed tomography expose objects concealed inside corrosion concretions, and tomography in particular transformed scholars' understanding of the Antikythera Mechanism.

## Conservation

Artifacts soaked in seawater decay quickly once they meet the air, so conservation starts the moment they are raised. Objects are kept wet and desalinated to draw out soluble salts. Waterlogged wood is usually strengthened with polyethylene glycol (PEG) and then freeze-dried or dried slowly in air; *Vasa* was sprayed with PEG for seventeen years, and conserving the *Mary Rose* hull took more than thirty. Iron and copper alloys are often stabilized by electrolytic reduction.

## Preservation In Situ

The 2001 UNESCO Convention on the Protection of the Underwater Cultural Heritage makes preservation in situ the first option to consider before any intervention. As a result, many projects now stress non-intrusive survey, protective reburial under sandbags or geotextiles, long-term monitoring of sediment movement and corrosion, and managed public access by way of underwater heritage trails. These steps address ongoing threats such as looting, commercial trawling and the climate-driven spread of wood-boring organisms.

Together, these methods reflect a wider shift in the discipline, away from treating recovery as a goal in itself and toward careful documentation, scientific interpretation and the long-term stewardship of submerged heritage.

**Nigerians Vote in Tight Presidential Race Amid Fears Over Disputed Result**

LAGOS, Nigeria — On Saturday, millions of Nigerians queued at polling stations to choose between President Goodluck Jonathan, the incumbent, and Muhammadu Buhari, a former military ruler, in a contest analysts describe as potentially the tightest since civilian rule returned in 1999.

Jonathan represents the People's Democratic Party (PDP), which has long dominated Nigerian politics. Buhari, a retired major general, heads the All Progressives Congress (APC), a coalition of opposition parties founded in 2013. This is the first time since military rule ended that an opposition candidate has been widely regarded as having a genuine chance of unseating a sitting president.

In many places voting began slowly, as election officials wrestled with new biometric card readers meant to reduce fraud. At his own polling unit in his home state of Bayelsa, Jonathan could not be verified by a card reader and was accredited by hand. The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) kept voting open into Sunday in some areas that suffered technical problems.

The election was first set for Feb. 14 but was delayed by six weeks after security chiefs said they could not ensure safety in the northeast. There, the Islamist militant group Boko Haram has fought a six-year insurgency that has killed thousands and uprooted over a million people.

Security has been the dominant theme of the campaign. Buhari, who briefly ruled Nigeria after a coup in the 1980s, has cast himself as a disciplined leader who can beat the insurgents and root out corruption. Jonathan's backers cite recent military gains against Boko Haram and economic growth under his administration, although lower oil prices have squeezed government revenue and weakened the naira.

The contest also mirrors Nigeria's longstanding regional and religious divides. Buhari is a Muslim and draws much of his backing from the largely Muslim north, whereas Jonathan, a Christian, is strongest in the south, including the oil-producing Niger Delta.

These divisions have raised fears that the losing camp may not accept the outcome. According to Human Rights Watch, rioting in parts of the north after the 2011 election, which Jonathan won against Buhari, left about 800 people dead.

Both candidates signed an accord in Abuja in January promising to campaign peacefully and honor the result, yet tension remains high. Some militants in the Niger Delta have cautioned that there could be unrest if Jonathan loses, and some Buhari supporters have pledged to resist any result they regard as rigged.

International observers, among them teams from the African Union and the European Union, are watching the vote, and world leaders have called on Nigerians to keep the process peaceful.

INEC chairman Attahiru Jega has said that results will be collated at the state level and then announced in Abuja, with official figures due in the next few days.

An outright win requires a simple majority of votes nationwide plus at least 25 percent of the vote in two-thirds of Nigeria's 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory.

The rotation of the Earth has no direct bearing on how long a flight takes. Because the atmosphere turns with the planet, an aircraft flies through air that is already moving at about the same speed as the ground beneath it. So an eastbound plane gets no boost from the Earth "turning beneath it," and a westbound plane suffers no penalty.

Rotation does matter indirectly, though. The Coriolis effect produced by the Earth's spin, combined with the temperature difference between the equator and the poles, helps create the jet streams, which are fast west-to-east rivers of air high in the atmosphere. In the mid-latitudes, eastbound flights can ride these tailwinds, while westbound flights have to push against them. That is why a New York to London flight usually takes about an hour less than the trip back.
